areas.name: Mine
areas.full_name: Mine (open-cut gibbsitic bauxite, India East Coast plateau type: clearing, topsoil and laterite-cap stripping, bench drill & blast, selective load & haul, ROM pad, primary sizing, grade control, dewatering, rehabilitation)
areas.purpose: Deliver on average ~5.9 Mt/yr wet (~5.3 Mt/yr dry) of run-of-mine (ROM) gibbsitic bauxite with controlled quality (available Al2O3, reactive SiO2) to the mine primary sizing station and overland conveyor. Tonnage mined equals refinery consumption plus or minus stock change. Mined land is rehabilitated progressively. DEPOSIT MODEL (fixed in this revision): India East Coast khondalite-plateau lateritic bauxite of the Panchpatmali / Baphlimali / Lanjigarh-supply type. The profile is topsoil 0.1-0.3 m, then a laterite/ferricrete cap 1-5 m, then a compact to hard bauxite horizon 10-30 m thick (design average ~12-18 m), then a lithomarge/kaolinitic clay floor (high reactive silica) over khondalite. Darling Range practice (thin 4-8 m friable ore, free-dig below a blasted caprock, ~60-110 ha/yr disturbance) is kept only as a comparison note.
areas.process_description: 1) Planning and grade control. Exploration drilling on a grid of about 60-120 m (in-fill to ~50 m) defines the ore body. Grade-control drilling uses RC on a ~12.5-25 m grid with 1 m intervals through the full ore column, supplemented by sampling of blast-hole cuttings on every bench. Samples are assayed by XRF and by a laboratory low-temperature caustic micro-digestion (~143-150 degC). This reports AVAILABLE Al2O3 (gibbsite alumina) and REACTIVE SiO2 (kaolinite silica, which forms desilication product in the refinery). Bench-by-bench ore/waste and grade-bin polygons are loaded into excavator GNSS guidance and the fleet management system (FMS). Grid spacings are engineering estimates. 2) Clearing. Dozers remove vegetation and merchantable timber; mulch is kept for rehabilitation. 3) Topsoil stripping. The top ~0.1-0.3 m, which holds the seed bank, is stripped separately and either returned directly to rehabilitation or stockpiled in low piles under 2 m high. 4) Laterite cap removal. The 1-5 m cap is ripped where it is soft or drilled and blasted where it is hard ferricrete. Depending on its available alumina and reactive silica, it is loaded either as waste (to backfill or dumps) or as low-grade ore for blending. Strip ratio is ~0.1-0.4 t waste per t ore (engineering estimate). 5) Ore benching by drill & blast (base case). The 10-30 m bauxite is mined on 5-8 m benches (2-4 benches per pit), with ramps no steeper than 8%. Holes are 115-165 mm DTH, pattern ~3.5 x 4.0 to 4.5 x 5.0 m, with 0.5-1.0 m subdrill. Powder factor is ~0.25-0.45 kg/bcm of bulk emulsion or ANFO, with electronic initiation. About 3.0-3.5 Mbcm/yr of ore plus hard cap is blasted, needing ~200-300 km/yr of drilling (engineering estimates). The lowest bench is stopped above the clay floor as directed by grade control, because the lithomarge is high in reactive silica. ALTERNATIVE: surface miners (Wirtgen 2200SM/2500SM class) cut the ore in 0.3-0.6 m layers without blasting. This is used near villages and forest, or where very selective floor control is needed. 6) Load and haul. 200-t class hydraulic backhoe excavators (and a 992-class wheel loader) load ~90-t rear-dump trucks. Trucks haul 2-6 km on engineered haul roads, either directly to the primary sizer dump hopper or to grade-bin fingers on the ROM pad. The FMS assigns trucks to faces so that the delivered blend meets targets: reactive SiO2 under the agreed ceiling, available Al2O3 over the floor. Mine roster is 2 x 12 h shifts, 7 days/week. Trucks achieve ~5,000-5,500 operating h/yr; production is lost on monsoon heavy-rain days. 7) Primary sizing. Trucks dump into a 2-sided hopper. An apron feeder draws ore into a twin-shaft primary sizer that reduces blasted ROM (top size ~1.0-1.5 m) to -200 mm for the 1,200 mm overland belt. Nominal rate is ~1,100-1,250 t/h over ~5,000-5,500 effective h/yr; the 1,800 t/h design gives surge capacity and allows pre-monsoon stock build. A pedestal rock breaker handles oversize. A self-cleaning magnet and metal detector protect the belts. 8) Dewatering and water management. Pits are rainfall-fed and deepen to 10-30 m, so the sumps collect large monsoon inflows. Diesel dry-prime pumps lift water to sediment ponds. Clean-water diversion drains route runoff around the pits, and haul roads are watered to suppress dust. 9) Rehabilitation. Because ore thickness (10-30 m) far exceeds waste volume, pits cannot be fully backfilled. Waste and cap are placed back on the pit floor, walls are reshaped to stable batters or left as benches, and topsoil is spread. The floor is deep-ripped on the contour and planted or seeded with local species. The final landform is a lowered plateau surface. Clearing to rehabilitation takes ~1-3 years per mining block. NOTES: Darling Range ore (~27-33% available Al2O3, quartz-rich, thin) gives a larger tonnage per t of alumina and is mostly free-dig. High-temperature (boehmitic) deposits such as Weipa or Guinea are mined similarly; the differences lie in the refinery, not the mine. Ore loss and dilution are an in-situ-to-ROM reconciliation only: dilution lowers the delivered grade, which is already reflected in the bauxite factor, and does not add tonnes to the refinery feed.

areas.layout_notes: Plateau-top deposit of ~10-20 km2 (life-of-mine reserves for ~30 years at ~5.9 Mt/yr). Mining proceeds in blocks of ~10-50 ha, irregular in plan, 10-30 m deep, on 5-8 m benches with 8% ramps. About 3 faces are active at any time for blending. Haul roads (22-25 m wide) radiate 2-6 km from a central semi-mobile primary sizing station at the plateau edge or centroid of ~5-10 years of reserves; the station is relocated about every 5-10 years. The ROM pad (4-6 ha) sits beside the dump-station ramp. Dump station: ramps rise ~8-10 m to the tipping deck on two sides (MSE walls); the sizer sits below with drives on both sides; MCC/e-house and transformer are ~20-30 m away. The mine infrastructure area (workshop, fuel farm, offices with mine control room, laboratory) is within ~1-3 km of the station on stable ground. The bulk explosives depot and magazines are isolated at their licensed separation distances. Sediment ponds are at low points down-gradient of the pits and pad. Communications towers are on high points. The field conveyor (A02) starts at the sizer and runs to the overland tail.

areas.name: Ore Transport
areas.full_name: Ore transport (mine to refinery overland conveyor system)
areas.purpose: Transport an average of ~5.9 Mt/yr of sized wet bauxite from the mine sizing station to the refinery stockyard over a generic ~20 km route (plateau to valley, assumed net fall ~150 m, i.e. ~0.75% average decline). The system must be reliable, low in operating cost and dust, and have a small land footprint. It is designed for 1,800 t/h so that it can catch up and build pre-monsoon stock.
areas.process_description: SELECTION: overland belt conveyor vs rail for 10-50 km. (a) Conveyor: continuous and electrically driven, so operating cost is low. Labour is low because it is operated remotely from the refinery CCR. It follows terrain with horizontal curves and grades up to ~15-18% (rail ~1-2%). Single loading and discharge points match a single mine and a single refinery. It is proven at this scale: ~50 km overland from the Boddington-area bauxite mine to the Worsley refinery (Wikipedia, 'Worsley Alumina'); ~14.6 km single-flight cable-belt conveyor from Panchpatmali mine to the Damanjodi refinery (verify); Alcoa's Huntly-Pinjarra and Willowdale-Wagerup overlands (lengths to verify); Channar 20 km iron-ore overland (Nordell 1991). (b) Rail: favoured above ~50-100 km, for multiple sources or customers, or where rail already exists. It needs a loop and loadout, a car dumper, rolling stock and crews, and flat gradients (heavy earthworks on plateau escarpments). (c) Slurry pipeline (e.g. Paragominas-Alunorte ~244 km): only for very long distances; requires wet grinding at the mine. DECISION: overland belt conveyor in 2 flights of ~10 km each. The intermediate transfer allows a lower belt rating and splits the risk. It is fed by a relocatable field conveyor (~2-5 km) from the semi-mobile sizer. Sequence: sized ore from 01-CV-001 -> 02-CV-001 field conveyor -> 02-CV-002 overland flight 1 -> intermediate transfer station 02-TS-001 -> 02-CV-003 overland flight 2 -> refinery junction tower -> 03-CV-001. POWER (corrected): the conveyor is NET MOTORING at all normal load cases. Artificial-friction resistance (ISO 5048 / DIN 22101, f ~0.012-0.016, moving mass ~220 kg/m) is ~1.2-1.6 MW per 10 km flight at design load. The gravity credit for a 75 m fall per flight is only ~0.37 MW, so absorbed power is ~0.9-1.4 MW per flight. Regeneration occurs only on local steep descending sections, transiently during stopping, or when only the downhill parts are loaded. Steady-state regeneration would require an average decline above ~2.8% (f x m_moving / m_load ~ 0.014 x 220/111). Active-front-end (AFE) VFDs are still specified for torque control, load sharing and absorbing that local or transient regenerative power. Controlled caliper brakes are required for safe stopping. A full dynamic (transient) analysis sets the start and stop ramps, take-up travel and brake sizing. It must include the loaded-downhill/empty-uphill and loaded-uphill/empty-downhill cases.

areas.name: Grinding
areas.purpose: Reduce crushed bauxite (-25 mm) to a pumpable caustic slurry (100 % < 1 mm, P80 ~250-400 um) in hot spent ('mill') liquor at a controlled bauxite-to-liquor charge, and buffer it ahead of pre-desilication. Grinding exposes the gibbsite and kaolinite surfaces so that desilication and the short low-temperature digestion go to completion. It also keeps the residue coarse enough to settle and wash. A04 is the single owner of the mill feed bins and weigh feeders; they are not duplicated in the stockyard area A03.
areas.process_description:
1) Blended crushed bauxite (-25 mm top size, ~10 % free moisture, F80 ~10-20 mm - engineering estimate) is reclaimed from the bauxite stockyard (A03) by belt conveyor. A shuttle/tripper distributes it to four mill feed bins: 3 grinding lines operating + 1 standby, each line rated for ~1/3 of plant feed plus ~10-15 % margin. Design dry feed is 640 t/h at a bauxite factor of 2.65 t/t, which is the plant-wide value.
2) A weigh-belt feeder under each bin meters ~213 t/h dry (~237 t/h wet) bauxite into the mill feed chute. Hot mill liquor is added in the feed chute: strong spent liquor, C ~270-290 g/L as Na2CO3, A/C ~0.36-0.38, heated to ~88-95 degC in the mill liquor heater using digestion blow-off vapour (A07). A ratio controller sets the liquor flow to the dry bauxite rate, with bauxite moisture compensation, to give ~50-55 % solids w/w in the mill. The total bauxite-to-caustic 'charge' across grinding and digestion liquor is the main lever on digester A/C. The dry feed rate is therefore measured very carefully: weightometer plus moisture analyser/lab moisture.
3) Wet overflow ball mills (nominal 4.4 m dia x 6.5 m EGL, ~2 MW) grind the ore with a graded ball charge (make-up ~75-90 mm). Hot caustic begins to react. A small part of the gibbsite dissolves: Al(OH)3 + NaOH -> NaAl(OH)4. Kaolinite (reactive silica) also starts to dissolve: Al2Si2O5(OH)4 + 6 NaOH -> 2 NaAl(OH)4 + 2 Na2SiO3 + H2O. Mill power and reaction raise the temperature by a few degC.
4) Mill discharge passes through a trommel bolted to the discharge trunnion. Scats go to a scats bunker: hard caprock/laterite lumps >~8-12 mm, tramp metal and worn balls. Slurry falls into the mill discharge pump box, where extra liquor brings it to ~45-48 % solids for screening.
5) Mill discharge pumps lift the slurry to a flow divider. There is one duty and one installed standby per mill, all hard-metal centrifugal slurry pumps. The divider feeds multi-deck high-frequency screens with 1.0 mm polyurethane panels on an elevated screen floor.
6) Screen oversize returns by gravity chute to the mill feed chute (closed circuit). Circulating load is ~80-150 % (engineering estimate). Screen undersize (product) flows by gravity launder to two agitated slurry storage tanks. Together they give ~4-5 h surge at design rate and decouple grinding from pre-desilication and digestion.
7) Slurry transfer pumps deliver ~830 m3/h of slurry to the pre-desilication heaters (A05) at a rate set by digestion feed demand. Slurry conditions: SG ~1.65-1.72, 44-48 % solids, ~85-93 degC.
Control philosophy:
- Charge control: bauxite dry tph and the liquor:bauxite ratio, fed forward from the digestion A/C target.
- Mill load: mill power, sound and bearing pressure.
- Pump-box level: VFD on the mill discharge pump.
- Product size: online PSD analyser plus shift sieve.
- Storage tank levels.
- Slurry density: radiometric or Coriolis.
High-temperature (boehmitic) plants: the grinding circuit is essentially the same. Lime is often added at the mill for titanate scale and phosphate control, and the grind may be finer.

areas.name: Pre-desilication
areas.purpose: Hold the ground bauxite slurry near its atmospheric boiling point (~98-102 degC) for ~8-10 h so that most of the reactive silica (kaolinite) dissolves and re-precipitates as sodalite-type desilication product (DSP) before digestion. This lowers dissolved silica in the digestion stream, which cuts DSP scale in the liquor heaters, slurry steam injectors and digesters and controls SiO2 in pregnant liquor (and therefore in product alumina). A05 also delivers the desilicated slurry from its 2 strings to the 3 digestion units through a common digestion feed tank.
areas.process_description:
1) Ground slurry (~85-93 degC) from storage (A04) is pumped in two parallel strings of ~415 m3/h each.
2) In each string a direct-contact steam-injection heater uses LP steam (~3.5-5 barg) to raise the slurry to 98-102 degC. The steam condenses directly into the slurry, adding ~15-30 t/h of water in total, which must later be removed in evaporation. The slurry boils at ~105-107 degC because of boiling-point elevation, so the tanks run atmospheric.
3) Slurry flows by gravity overflow through three agitated, insulated tanks in series per string (6 tanks, ~1,500 m3 working each). Both strings then overflow into a common agitated digestion feed tank (05-TK-007, ~1,000 m3 working). Nominal residence is ~11-12 h with all tanks on line and ~9-10 h with one desilication tank out for descaling (engineering estimate; typical practice 6-12 h).
4) Chemistry. Kaolinite dissolves: Al2Si2O5(OH)4 + 6 NaOH -> 2 NaAl(OH)4 + 2 Na2SiO3 + H2O. The dissolved silica reacts with aluminate to precipitate sodalite: 6 Na2SiO3 + 6 NaAl(OH)4 + Na2X -> Na6[Al6Si6O24].Na2X + 12 NaOH + 6 H2O, where X = CO3(2-), SO4(2-), 2Cl-, 2OH- etc. It is often written 3(Na2O.Al2O3.2SiO2.nH2O).Na2X. The DSP stays with the residue. Stoichiometrically, each tonne of reactive SiO2 locks up ~0.85 t Al2O3 and ~0.69 t Na2O (as Na8 sodalite), which is why reactive silica is the main driver of caustic consumption. At design 2 % reactive SiO2 (~12.8 t/h SiO2) this is ~34 t/h DSP, with ~11 t/h Al2O3 and ~9 t/h Na2O lost (engineering estimate). Target: ~70-90 % of reactive silica converted to DSP before digestion; the rest completes in digestion. Quartz is essentially inert at <= 150 degC.
5) Desilication rate improves with temperature, time, DSP seed (recycled solids) and fine grind. Low caustic slows it.
6) Desilicated slurry (~44-47 % solids, ~860 m3/h, 98-102 degC) leaves 05-TK-007 to the digestion slurry charge pump trains of the three digestion units (A06), one train per unit. Each train takes ~287 m3/h from a common suction header.
High-temperature plants: pre-desilication is similar, but much of the desilication also occurs in the high-temperature digesters, and some plants use pressure pre-desilication at higher temperature.

The dissolved silica reacts with aluminate to precipitate sodalite: 6 Na2SiO3 + 6 NaAl(OH)4 + Na2X -> Na6[Al6Si6O24].Na2X + 12 NaOH + 6 H2O, where X = CO3(2-), SO4(2-), 2Cl-, 2OH- etc. It is often written 3(Na2O.Al2O3.2SiO2.nH2O).Na2X. The DSP stays with the residue. Stoichiometrically, each tonne of reactive SiO2 locks up ~0.85 t Al2O3 and ~0.69 t Na2O (as Na8 sodalite), which is why reactive silica is the main driver of caustic consumption. At design 2 % reactive SiO2 (~12.8 t/h SiO2) this is ~34 t/h DSP, with ~11 t/h Al2O3 and ~9 t/h Na2O lost (engineering estimate). Target: ~70-90 % of reactive silica converted to DSP before digestion; the rest completes in digestion. Quartz is essentially inert at <= 150 degC.
Desilication rate improves with temperature, time, DSP seed (recycled solids) and fine grind. Low caustic slows it.

areas.name: Digestion
areas.purpose: Dissolve the gibbsite in the bauxite into hot caustic liquor at ~145 degC (low-temperature digestion), raising liquor A/C from ~0.37 (spent) to ~0.70-0.74. Thermal efficiency comes from regenerative heating of the spent liquor stream with flash vapour, final indirect heating of the liquor with live steam, and direct live-steam injection into the slurry stream. This 'double-stream' arrangement with liquor-only indirect heating is the base case for the reference plant (CHANGED from the draft, which also had flash-vapour slurry heaters and PD pumps; those are now a documented option only).
areas.process_description:
Design basis: double-stream regenerative low-temperature digestion. There are 3 parallel digestion units, each ~1/3 of plant capacity (~80 t/h Al2O3). The unit count is an engineering estimate; real low-temperature refineries of this size use 2-5 units. Per unit:
1) Slurry stream. ~287 m3/h of desilicated slurry (~44-47 % solids, ~100 degC) is taken from the digestion feed tank 05-TK-007. Two hard-metal centrifugal slurry pumps in series (one duty train + one standby train) raise it to ~12-14 barg. Two in-line direct live-steam injection heaters in series (06-SI) then heat it from ~100 degC to ~130-140 degC (design ~138). No slurry heat-transfer surfaces are used, which avoids the rapid DSP/kaolinite fouling that slurry tube heaters suffer.
2) Liquor stream. Strong spent liquor from evaporation (~700-730 m3/h per unit, C ~270-290 g/L as Na2CO3, A/C ~0.37, ~90-100 degC) is pumped by high-head centrifugal liquor pumps (~15-20 barg) through 6 flash-vapour LIQUOR HEATERS (liquor in tubes, flash vapour on shell, stage 6 -> 1) to ~128-131 degC. Two LIVE-STEAM LIQUOR HEATERS (MP steam 10-12 barg, ~184-192 degC) then take it to ~158-166 degC (design 162). The liquor is therefore 'superheated' relative to the digestion temperature.
3) Both streams enter digester 1 through a mixing inlet. The heat in the superheated liquor plus the slurry injection steam brings the mixture to 143-150 degC (design 145) after the gibbsite dissolution endotherm. The slurry injection steam rate is the fine temperature trim (TIC on digester 1/2 outlet).
4) The slurry flows under pressure through 4 agitated digesters in series. Residence is ~55-60 min with all 4 on line and ~40-45 min with one bypassed. Main reaction: Al(OH)3(s) + NaOH(aq) -> NaAl(OH)4(aq). Gibbsite dissolution is endothermic (~0.45-0.55 GJ/t Al2O3 dissolved - engineering estimate, verify) and fast at 145 degC, typically complete within ~10-30 min. DSP precipitation completes. Quartz, hematite, goethite and anatase stay largely unreacted; quartz attack is negligible at <= 150 degC, a key advantage of low-temperature digestion. BOEHMITE in gibbsitic ore (typically ~0.5-5 % of the bauxite, e.g. Darling Range and some India East Coast ores) is largely NOT extracted at 145 degC. It reports to residue and is counted in total Al2O3 but not in available Al2O3. Undissolved boehmite (and hematite/goethite surfaces) can seed 'boehmite reversion' of dissolved alumina once the liquor becomes supersaturated on cooling. The time from blow-off to settler overflow (A07-A08) is therefore kept short, and digester exit A/C is held below the reversion-risk limit. Part of the organic carbon (humates) degrades to oxalate, carbonate and low-MW organics. Digester exit liquor A/C is ~0.70-0.74.
5) Digested slurry (~980-1,040 m3/h per unit, ~145 degC) is let down into the flash train (A07). Flash vapour from stages 1-6 returns to the liquor heaters. The surplus atmospheric blow-off vapour goes to the A04 mill liquor heater and the A07 surface vent condensers or evaporation.
Heat balance per unit (engineering estimate). Demand ~68-72 MW:
- liquor 95 -> 145 degC: ~43 MW
- slurry 100 -> 145 degC: ~14 MW
- dissolution endotherm: ~10-12 MW
- losses: ~1.5 MW
Flash vapour recovered in the liquor heaters is ~30 MW. The liquor heat sink is limited to <~131 degC by the flash vapour temperatures, and the liquor's heat-capacity flow (~0.87 MW/K) is smaller than that of the digested slurry (~1.29 MW/K). Live steam therefore supplies ~38-42 MW: liquor heaters ~27-30 MW (~48-55 t/h) and slurry injection ~9-12 MW (~15-22 t/h), ~65-75 t/h per unit in total. This is ~0.8-0.95 t steam/t Al2O3, vs ~0.55-0.7 t/t with the slurry-heater option.
Operating pressure: digester 1 is held at ~6-7 barg. That is above the vapour pressure of the incoming 162 degC liquor (~4.6 barg with BPE ~6 K) and well above the mixture vapour pressure at 145 degC (~2.5-3 barg). The last digester runs at ~5-6.5 barg under PIC on the let-down valve. Design: 10 barg at 200 degC (CHANGED from 9 barg/175 degC - see 06-DG).
Sweetening: not used in this base design (the bauxite is essentially all gibbsite). In plants that digest mixed gibbsite/boehmite ore at high temperature, extra gibbsitic slurry ('sweetening') is injected into the hot digested slurry in the first flash stages to raise A/C. Mention for trainees only.
High-temperature (boehmitic/diasporic) plants differ:
- 230-280 degC at ~30-60 barg, with PD (GEHO-type) pumps to 60-100+ bar
- slurry heaters (shell & tube or tube-in-tube) with 8-12+ flash stages
- tube digesters or autoclaves with indirect heating (molten salt in some plants)
- lime addition to control titanate scale
- quartz attack and higher caustic loss; boehmite/titanate scales

areas.name: Flash Cooling & Heat Recovery
areas.purpose: Cool the digested slurry from ~145 degC to its atmospheric boiling point (~106-107 degC) in pressure steps. Each step produces flash vapour at a successively lower pressure, which heats the incoming spent liquor (regenerative heat recovery). Collect the condensate for reuse, and route the surplus atmospheric blow-off vapour to useful sinks or surface vent condensers. Deliver the blow-off slurry to the A08 sand cyclones with a single pumping step.
areas.process_description:
1) Digested slurry from the last digester is let down through a severe-service control valve (which holds digester pressure) into flash tank 1.
2) In each of 6 pressurised flash tanks per unit the pressure is below the vapour pressure of the incoming slurry. Part of the water boils instantly (flashes) until the slurry cools to the boiling temperature at that pressure. In the liquor-only base case the slurry cools ~3.9-4 K per pressurised stage, and ~0.55-0.6 % of its mass evaporates per stage (fraction = cp x dT / hfg = 3.15 x 4 / 2,180).
3) Vapour leaves each tank top through a disengagement space/baffle to the paired liquor heater in A06. Slurry from the tank bottom passes through a level-control (let-down) valve to the next, lower-pressure tank.
4) Indicative stage table (engineering estimate; slurry exit T / vapour saturation T / pressure):
- FT1: 141 / 135 degC, ~3.13 bar a (~2.1 barg)
- FT2: 137 / 131 degC, ~2.78 bar a
- FT3: 133.5 / 127.5 degC, ~2.51 bar a
- FT4: 129.5 / 123.5 degC, ~2.22 bar a
- FT5: 125.5 / 119.5 degC, ~1.95 bar a
- FT6: 121.5 / 115.5 degC, ~1.72 bar a (~0.7 barg)
- Atmospheric blow-off tank: ~106-107 degC
The vapour is saturated at a lower temperature than the slurry because the caustic liquor has a boiling-point elevation of ~5-7 K. Pressures are from IAPWS-IF97. CHANGED from the draft table (139/133 ... 109/103 degC), which assumed paired slurry + liquor heaters.
5) Blow-off (atmospheric) tank. With liquor-only heating the liquor (~0.87 MW/K) cannot absorb all the heat released by the slurry (~1.29 MW/K) at temperatures below ~131 degC. The final flash from ~121.5 to ~106 degC is therefore large: ~30-33 t/h vapour per unit (~1.8-2 % of slurry mass), ~90-100 t/h in total. Over all stages to atmospheric, ~5.5-6 % of the slurry mass evaporates. Blow-off vapour goes to:
(a) the A04 mill liquor heater (~13-20 t/h total);
(b) as an option to be confirmed by A18, an intermediate evaporator effect;
(c) the rest to surface (shell & tube) vent condensers on cooling water, which recover the condensate.
The slurry is pumped by 07-PP-001..006 directly to the A08 sand cyclones. Cyclone overflow goes to the A08 dilution/settler feed tank, where it is diluted with first-washer overflow. Residence from blow-off to settler overflow is kept short to limit boehmite/gibbsite reversion.
6) Condensate. Liquor heater condensate from each stage drains via condensate pots and cascades to the next lower-pressure pot, re-flashing. It is finally collected as 'process condensate' (~50 t/h per unit), together with the vent-condenser and mill-liquor-heater condensate (~25-33 t/h per unit). The total is ~230-250 t/h (~0.95-1.0 t/t Al2O3). It is monitored by conductivity for caustic contamination and sent to the plant process condensate tank (18-TK-012, owned by A18) for residue/hydrate washing or polishing. Live-steam condensate is kept separate ('clean condensate') and returned to the boilers after conductivity checks.
7) Non-condensable gases from the heater shells are bled stage to stage. The last stage and the blow-off tank vent to the vent condensers (odour/VOC control).
8) Scale control. Gibbsite (from alumina supersaturation as the slurry cools) and DSP scale form on flash tank walls, inlet boxes and interstage lines/valves. These are inspected and descaled at unit shutdowns (~6-12 months, engineering estimate) by UHP water jetting or mechanical means, and erosion-resistant inserts are replaced.
High-temperature plants: typically 8-12+ flash stages from ~250 degC, much higher first-stage pressures (~20-30 bar), and titanate/boehmite scales.

areas.name: Sand Removal, Settling & Washing
areas.full_name: Sand removal, settling & washing (clarification and CCD residue washing)
areas.purpose: Separate the coarse sand and the fine residue (red mud) from the digested slurry. Deliver a clear pregnant (green) liquor to security filtration (A10). Recover soluble soda and dissolved alumina from the residue by counter-current decantation (CCD) washing before the residue is filtered (A09). Provide the area spill-recovery system and the refinery process-spill (emergency) catchment pond.
areas.process_description:
1) FEED: Digested slurry leaves the atmospheric blow-off tank of digestion (A07) at about 103-108 degC, close to its boiling point. It is supersaturated in alumina (A/C about 0.70-0.74) and carries about 95-110 g/L residue solids (about 285 t/h dry residue in about 2,750-2,950 m3/h liquor). The 08-PP-001 cyclone feed pumps are the ONLY pumping step between the A07 blow-off tank and the settlers. The separate A07 blow-off pump to the dilution tank is deleted, and the sand cyclones sit upstream of the settler feed (dilution) tank. A08 must be fast: from the digester to the end of security filtration the liquor is metastable. Gibbsite can autoprecipitate in settlers, tanks and launders, which loses product and builds scale, so residence time is kept short and temperature high.
2) SAND REMOVAL: The cyclone feed pumps send the slurry to two clusters of hydrocyclones that cut at about 100-150 um. Underflow (sand: quartz, coarse goethite/hematite and laterite gravel) drops to a 3-stage counter-current screw-classifier train and is washed with hot wash water. Washed sand is dewatered on a vibrating screen and conveyed to a stockpile for RSA drainage layers and roads. Cyclone overflow (fine residue plus liquor) flows to the settler feed tank. Sand content depends strongly on the ore. The DESIGN ORE is India East Coast (khondalite) gibbsitic bauxite, which is low in quartz (total SiO2 about 2-5%), so sand is about 3-8% of residue, about 9-23 t/h. The circuit is sized for a 45 t/h maximum to absorb ore variability. Darling Range ore gives roughly 40-50% of residue as quartz-rich sand and would need a sand circuit about 5-10 times larger, with multiple classifier trains. With East Coast ore there is too little sand for embankment construction, so RSA embankments use compacted residue and borrow (see A09).
3) DILUTION AND FLOCCULATION: First-washer (W1) overflow, the weak liquor at about 130-170 g/L C as Na2CO3, dilutes the cyclone overflow in the settler feed tank. This lowers viscosity and sets pregnant-liquor C (target about 240-255 g/L as Na2CO3) and A/C (0.68-0.72). Flocculant is added in stages. Hydroxamate-modified polyacrylamide goes in first, for overflow clarity: it captures fine iron and titanium minerals and DSP. High-MW sodium polyacrylate follows for settling rate. Both are dosed into the feed pipe and feedwell.
4) SETTLING (clarification): High-rate settlers (decanters) separate residue from liquor. Overflow is pregnant (green) liquor at about 10-50 mg/L suspended solids, about 100-105 degC, going to security filtration (A10). Underflow at about 30-40 wt% solids is pumped to the Washer 1 feedwell.
5) CCD WASHING: Six washer stages operate in series and a 7th is installed for descaling rotation. Mud moves forward (W1 to W6) by underflow pumping. Wash liquor moves backward. Hot wash water (RSA return water, process condensate and press filtrate, about 500-650 m3/h) enters W6. Each washer's overflow joins the feed of the washer before it, and W1 overflow returns to the settler feed tank. A side-stream of W1/W2 overflow (about 500 m3/h) goes to causticisation (A19) and returns with carbonate converted to caustic. Soluble Na2O and Al2O3 concentrations fall stage by stage (ideal-mixing model). Final underflow leaves W6 at 45-55 wt% solids with residual liquor of about 3-8 g/L total soda as Na2CO3 and is pumped to residue filtration (A09).
6) CHEMISTRY in this area: (a) Supersaturated pregnant liquor can revert, Al(OH)4- -> Al(OH)3 + OH-. Hot liquor and short residence prevent this. (b) Desilication product (DSP, sodalite type Na8[Al6Si6O24]X2 with X = 2OH-, CO3 2-, SO4 2- or Cl-) has largely formed in pre-desilication and digestion and leaves with the mud. It is the main CHEMICAL soda loss: about 0.69 t Na2O per t reactive SiO2 (sodalite stoichiometry), about 37 kg Na2O/t alumina at 2% reactive silica. Washing cannot recover it. (c) Washing recovers only SOLUBLE soda carried in the liquor that wets the mud. (d) In the later washers, where liquor is weaker and cooler, some gibbsite can precipitate (soluble alumina loss), and calcium carbonate and oxalate scale can form. Washer temperature control and rotation of the spare washer manage this.
7) WATER BALANCE: Net water added in A08 is wash water minus W6 underflow liquor, about 550 - 280 = about 270 t/h. All of it ends up in the liquor circuit and must be removed by evaporation (A18). The wash ratio therefore trades soda recovery against evaporator steam. This is a key point for trainees. Underflow density is the stronger lever: a denser underflow improves washing without adding water.
8) SPILL CONTAINMENT: Each thickener and pump bay is bunded and drains to area sumps (08-PP-031). The sumps return strong spills to the settler feed or W1 and dilute spills to the wash water tank. A refinery process-spill catchment pond (08-PD-001) receives a full thickener inventory after loss of containment, overflow from bunds in a design storm, and drain-downs that the spare thickener cannot take.

areas.name: Residue Filtration & Storage
areas.purpose: Dewater washed residue to a high-solids filter cake for dry stacking, with cake washing to minimise soluble soda and alkalinity. Transport the cake to a lined, engineered residue storage area (dry stack) managed to GISTM/ICOLD/ANCOLD practice, and return alkaline water to the refinery so no untreated discharge leaves site.
areas.process_description:
1) FILTER FEED: W6 underflow (about 285 t/h dry normal, 310 t/h design, at 45-55 wt% solids and 3-8 g/L soda as Na2CO3) goes to two agitated filter feed tanks, one per press building, with about 10-14 h combined buffer.
2) PRESS FILTRATION: Recessed-chamber membrane filter presses (2.0 x 2.0 m plates, about 1,000 m2 each) are filled by dedicated feed pumps at rising pressure up to about 7-10 bar g (engineering estimate). The cake is optionally washed with hot water to displace residual liquor, membrane-squeezed at about 15-16 bar g and briefly air-blown. Plates are then opened and the cake drops onto conveyors below. A complete cycle (close, fill, squeeze, wash, blow, open, plate shift and discharge of about 140 chambers, periodic cloth wash) takes about 60-90 min. Each press holds about 20 m3 of cake per cycle (1,000 m2 / 2 x 0.04 m), about 28-30 t dry, so it delivers about 20-25 t/h dry. 14 operating presses + 2 standby (16 installed, in two buildings of 8) cover the 310 t/h design. Cake reaches about 70-78 wt% solids (22-30% moisture). Published references: press cake >70% solids (IAI 2015); Alunorte about 22% moisture; CHALCO Zhongzhou 27-30% moisture with 600-800 m2 presses; typical 23-27% moisture (Wikipedia, Red mud). Vendor pilot press tests on project residue are required before final sizing.
3) FILTRATE: Filtrate (low soda) is collected and returned as wash water to the CCD (08-TK-021). This closes the soda loop.
4) CAKE HANDLING: Under-press belts collect each batch drop and transfer it via collector conveyors to a truck loadout bin. Articulated dump trucks haul it 2-5 km (engineering estimate) to the active RSA cell. An overland conveyor with mobile stacker is the main alternative at about 3.2 Mt/yr wet.
5) DRY STACKING AND MUD FARMING: Cake is spread in thin layers of about 0.3-0.5 m by dozer, turned and conditioned by amphirol and/or harrow to speed drying and atmospheric carbonation, then compacted. Thin-layer stacking uses 0.3-0.5 m layers dried to about 70% solids before the next layer; EGA Al Taweelah places residue in 300 mm layers with 5 m lifts (IAI 2015).
6) NEUTRALISATION / ALKALINITY REDUCTION, base case: (a) cake washing in the press; (b) atmospheric carbonation of the stack surface during farming, CO2 + 2OH- -> CO3 2- + H2O and Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O -> 2NaHCO3, with tricalcium aluminate and other alkaline solids buffering pH so it falls only gradually; (c) all lake water and underdrainage returned to the refinery. Option with a CO2 source (space provided): CO2 carbonation of filter feed (Alcoa Kwinana concept; reported pH reduction from about 13 to about 10.5 using CO2 from a neighbouring ammonia plant, not retrieved this session). Option for a coastal site: seawater neutralisation of residue or lake water. Mg2+ and Ca2+ in seawater precipitate the hydroxide and carbonate alkalinity as brucite, hydrotalcite and calcite, giving pH about 8-8.5 (IAI 2015; QAL supernatant <8.5 pH, <30 mg/L solids, <5 mg/L Al, 50 m diffuser).
7) RSA: The stack is built in cells on a composite-lined base (HDPE geomembrane over compacted low-permeability clay), with a drainage blanket and slotted pipes to sumps, perimeter starter embankments of compacted borrow, later raises of compacted residue, upstream or centreline raises in 2-5 m lifts, a decant/stormwater pond (residue lake), seepage interception and groundwater bores. With the low-sand East Coast design ore (about 0.07-0.19 Mt/yr sand), washed sand covers only part of the drainage blanket, so imported gravel/sand and compacted residue are needed for drains and embankments. Governance follows the Global Industry Standard on Tailings Management (GISTM, 2020: 6 topic areas, 15 principles, 77 requirements), ICOLD bulletins on tailings dams and ANCOLD Guidelines on Tailings Dams. Consequence classification uses GISTM Annex 2.
8) Wet disposal (lagooning at 18-22% solids, IAI 2015), historically common in India and worldwide, is NOT selected because of footprint, seepage and dam-break risk (Ajka 2010: about 1 Mm3 released, 10 deaths).

areas.name: Security Filtration
areas.purpose: Remove the last fine residue particles (iron and titanium minerals, DSP) from the settler overflow so that the pregnant liquor sent to heat interchange and precipitation is practically solids-free. This protects alumina purity (Fe2O3, SiO2 and TiO2 in smelter-grade alumina) and prevents fouling of the heat interchangers.
areas.process_description:
1) Settler overflow (green liquor, about 10-50 mg/L solids, about 100-105 degC) flows by gravity to the unfiltered liquor tank. Security filter feed pumps deliver it to a bank of horizontal pressure leaf filters (Kelly type).
2) FILTER AID: Tricalcium aluminate (TCA, Ca3[Al(OH)6]2, also written 3CaO.Al2O3.6H2O) is made on site by reacting slaked lime with aluminate liquor: 3Ca(OH)2 + 2Al(OH)4- -> Ca3[Al(OH)6]2 + 2OH-. TCA forms hard hexagonal/cubic crystals that make a porous, incompressible precoat and cake.
3) CYCLE (engineering estimate): (a) fill the filter with liquor; (b) precoat by recirculating TCA slurry until the filtrate is clear (about 10-20 min); (c) filter with TCA body feed until differential pressure reaches about 3-4 bar or the time limit (about 4-12 h); (d) drain the heel back to the feed tank; (e) sluice cake off the leaves with dilute liquor sprays while the sluice header oscillates; (f) send the sluiced slurry to the cake tank and pump it back to the settler feed tank or Washer 1, so residue and TCA leave via the CCD; (g) return to service. Leaves are periodically pulled and cloths descaled or replaced.
4) Filtrate turbidity is monitored on each filter. Filtered pregnant liquor goes to the filtered liquor tank and then to heat interchange (A11) at 98-104 degC.
5) Target filtrate solids < about 5-10 mg/L, typically < 5 mg/L (engineering estimate). The trade-off is TCA dosing: lime consumption plus a small alumina loss to TCA.

areas.name: Heat Interchange
areas.purpose: Cool polished pregnant (green) liquor from ~98-104 degC to the precipitation fill temperature (72-78 degC for the agglomeration stage). The heat is recovered into cold spent liquor, which returns to A18 evaporation and liquor blending and from there to A06 digestion. A11 also holds the spent-liquor surge tank, a cooling-water trim cooler for tight control of the fill temperature, the cooled-PL split to agglomeration and seed repulping, and the hot-caustic clean-in-place (CIP) system for the exchangers. The temperature set here is the main lever on precipitation supersaturation, agglomeration and particle-size control.
areas.process_description: 1) Polished pregnant liquor (PL) arrives from the A10 security/polishing filtrate tank at 98-104 degC (aligned with A10). Typical composition is C ~240-255 g/L as Na2CO3, A/C 0.68-0.72 and suspended solids <10 mg/L. Four feed pumps (3 operating, 1 standby) send it through duplex basket strainers. 2) The PL passes counter-current through banks of gasketed plate heat exchangers (PHEs) against spent liquor from the A11 spent-liquor tank (55-62 degC). Six PHEs carry the duty and two are offline at any time for hot-caustic cleaning. The PL leaves at 76-82 degC and the spent liquor at 82-90 degC. The duty is ~80-100 MW for a PL flow of ~3,000-3,300 m3/h (engineering estimate: rho ~1.30 t/m3, cp ~3.2-3.3 kJ/kg.K, dT ~22-25 K; ~3.5-3.9 MW per K). 3) The regenerative PHEs cannot cool the PL below what the spent-liquor inlet temperature and approach allow. The rest of the cooling is done in a cooling-water trim cooler (1 operating + 1 standby), which sets the agglomeration fill temperature to ±0.5-1 degC. The fill temperature is a cascade master over both the trim-cooler cooling-water valve and a PL bypass valve around the trim cooler. 4) Downstream of the trim cooler the cooled-PL header splits three ways. About 2,000-2,600 m3/h goes to the A12 agglomeration distribution box. About 500-900 m3/h goes to the A13 coarse-seed repulp tanks. About 100-200 m3/h goes to the A13 fine-seed tank. Each split is flow-controlled; all values are engineering estimates. 5) Chemistry: as PL cools, the gibbsite equilibrium solubility A* falls steeply, so the liquor becomes supersaturated. Relative supersaturation is (A - A*)/C. Some gibbsite nucleates heterogeneously on the cooled PL-side plate surfaces, so the PL side of the PHEs scales with gibbsite in days. The spent side is undersaturated in gibbsite as it is heated and scales much more slowly, mainly with DSP (sodium aluminosilicate) and oxalate. Gibbsite scale is redissolved by circulating hot, strong, low-A/C liquor (A18 strong liquor, C ~300-320 g/L, A/C ~0.36-0.38, heated to 90-100 degC) for 2-6 h on a rotating schedule. 6) The heated spent liquor goes to A18 (evaporator feed and digestion-liquor blending; A18 owns the split between evaporation, ~1,700 m3/h, and the bypass to the blend tank). 7) Low-temperature (gibbsitic) and high-temperature (boehmitic) plants differ only slightly here. In a high-temperature plant the PL leaves the flash train and clarification at a similar ~100-106 degC, so the interchange duty is similar. Its higher digestion A/C (0.72-0.75+) gives a higher precipitation driving force. European high-caustic single-stage plants cool further (to a ~60-65 degC fill) to make floury or high-yield hydrate, and many older and high-temperature plants cool PL by multi-stage vacuum flash instead of PHEs.

areas.name: Precipitation
areas.purpose: Crystallise gibbsite (Al(OH)3) from the cooled, supersaturated pregnant liquor onto recycled seed, in order to (a) recover alumina (yield ~75-85 g/L Al2O3, design ~80 g/L), (b) produce hydrate with the size distribution, strength and soda needed for sandy smelter-grade alumina, and (c) return spent liquor (A/C ~0.36-0.39) to the liquor circuit. Design: Australian-style two-stage process. A hot agglomeration stage with a low charge of fine seed is followed by a growth stage with a high charge of coarse seed and interstage cooling.
areas.process_description: Chemistry: Na+ + Al(OH)4- (aq) -> Al(OH)3 (s, gibbsite) + Na+ + OH-. This is the reverse of gibbsite digestion. It is slow and seeded, and is driven by supersaturation (A - A*), where A* is the gibbsite equilibrium solubility. A* falls with temperature and rises with caustic concentration (Rosenberg and Healy 1996 solubility model). The growth rate is roughly second order in supersaturation, with an activation energy of ~60 kJ/mol (Misra and White 1971). Crystallisation is exothermic: the heat of precipitation is of the order of 20-30 kJ/mol Al(OH)3 (engineering estimate, verify against the plant heat balance), i.e. ~25-35 MW at the design rate. Together with the required ~15-20 K fall in temperature, this heat is removed by the interstage coolers (45-70 MW) and by ambient losses from uninsulated tanks and launders (~15-30 MW, engineering estimate). Three mechanisms act together: (i) secondary nucleation creates new fine particles (<1-5 µm) and is favoured by low temperature and high supersaturation; (ii) agglomeration cements fine particles into ~20-60 µm agglomerates and is favoured by high temperature (>70 degC), high supersaturation and low seed surface area; (iii) growth deposits layers on existing surfaces and controls the yield. STEP 1, agglomeration stage (2 lines x 3 tanks): cooled PL at 72-78 degC from A11 (~2,000-2,600 m3/h, the balance of PL after the seed-repulp side-streams) is split equally to the two lines at a distribution box. Washed fine seed from A13 (fine seed charge ~30-80 g/L of agglomeration PL, engineering estimate) is added to tank AG-1. High supersaturation with little seed area promotes agglomeration of the fines into strong mosaic particles. Residence is ~7-11 h (engineering estimate, 5-6 tanks online, ~2,200-2,900 m3/h slurry). STEP 2, growth stage (2 lines x 13 tanks, 12 operating per line): coarse seed from A13 (filtered cake repulped in a PL side-stream; charge ~350-600 g/L on total PL, ~10-25 m2/L seed area, engineering estimate) enters G-1. Slurry flows through the tanks in series by bottom-draw airlifts and roof-level launders. Two interstage cooling stations per line (after G-4 and G-8) take the temperature from ~70-74 degC at G-1 to ~55-60 degC at G-13, maintaining supersaturation as A falls and maximising yield. Growth slurry flow is the total PL plus seed solids volume plus seed-cake liquor, ~3,700-4,400 m3/h (~1,850-2,200 m3/h per line). Through 24 operating growth tanks (~108,000 m3) this gives a growth residence of ~24-29 h, or ~23-28 h after an allowance for volume lost to wall scale. Total precipitation residence is ~31-38 h. CHANGE from the earlier draft: one growth tank per line was added (G-13), because 22 operating x 4,500 m3 gave only ~21-25 h once the seed volume was counted. The target spent A/C of 0.36-0.38 at this residence and end temperature must be confirmed with a precipitation model (open question). STEP 3: slurry from G-13 (A/C ~0.36-0.39, solids ~450-700 g/L on a liquor basis, ~33-40% w/w) gravitates to A13 classification. A crystal growth modifier (CGM, a surfactant/oil emulsion) may be dosed to suppress fines and coarsen the product. Precipitation needs no extra heat: the falling temperature profile is set by A11 and the interstage coolers. One tank per line is normally bypassed in rotation for descaling. Removed gibbsite scale is crushed at a scale pad and returned to A04 grinding/digestion, where it dissolves readily as high-grade, silica-free alumina. Contrast with European 'floury' or high-yield practice: higher caustic (~300 g/L), lower fill temperature (~60-65 degC), single stage, finer product. Boehmitic (high-temperature) plants use the same precipitation principles but can reach a higher PL A/C, so yield is higher for the same spent A/C.

areas.name: Classification & Seed
areas.purpose: Separate the end-of-precipitation hydrate by size into (1) coarse product hydrate (to A14 filtration and A15 calcination), (2) coarse (growth) seed recycled to G-1, and (3) fine seed recycled to agglomeration after washing to remove co-precipitated sodium oxalate. A13 also recovers clear spent liquor (thickener overflow) for A11. Classification sets the product PSD and the seed balance.
areas.process_description: 1) G-13 slurry from each line (~1,850-2,200 m3/h, 450-700 g/L solids, 55-60 degC) flows by gravity launder into a primary cyclone feed tank (one per line). 2) Primary classification: slurry pumps feed a primary cyclone cluster. The cut size d50c is ~80-110 µm (engineering estimate), set so that the underflow solids rate equals the product rate (~370-420 t/h total). Underflow (coarsest particles, ~55-65% w/w solids) goes to the A14 product slurry tanks. Overflow goes to a secondary cyclone feed tank. 3) Secondary classification: secondary cyclones (finer cut, d50c ~40-60 µm, engineering estimate) produce an underflow of coarse seed (~1,050-1,800 t/h) and an overflow carrying fines (<~45 µm) and most of the liquor. 4) Coarse seed is dewatered on vacuum disc filters to remove spent liquor, which would otherwise dilute the supersaturation in growth. The cake is repulped with a cooled-PL side-stream (~500-900 m3/h from A11) in coarse seed repulp tanks and pumped to G-1. Because these tanks hold supersaturated PL in contact with a large seed area, they act as small precipitators and scale, so they are descaled on the same cycle as the precipitators. 5) Secondary overflow (~1,900-2,600 m3/h) goes to two tertiary (fine seed) thickeners. areas.name: Hydrate Filtration
areas.purpose: Filter the product hydrate (primary cyclone underflow), wash out entrained spent liquor with hot condensate to minimise soluble soda carried to calcination and to recover caustic, and deliver a cake of ~6-10% free moisture to the A15 calciner hydrate storage at ~370-420 t/h dry. Weak wash filtrate returns to the liquor circuit (spent-liquor tank or residue washing, per the plant water balance). 5) The cake is dewatered by air drawn through it (dry zone), then discharged by a helical scroll to a collecting conveyor. areas.name: Calcination
areas.purpose: Turn washed product hydrate (gibbsite, Al(OH)3) into smelter-grade alumina (SGA). Two identical gas suspension calciner trains with holding vessels (GSC-HV) dry, dehydrate (calcine) and cool it. The area also holds a product-hydrate slurry buffer so that a calciner outage does not force an immediate cut in refinery output. Calcination sets product LOI, BET surface area and alpha-alumina content. It cannot remove soda or fix weak particles: Na2O and particle size come from precipitation and hydrate washing (A13/A14). This is the refinery's largest single fuel user and CO2 source.
areas.process_description:
TECHNOLOGY CHOICE: The reference plant uses the FLSmidth-type Gas Suspension Calciner with Holding Vessel (GSC-HV), 2 trains x 3,500 t/d nameplate. The alternative is the Metso Outotec (ex-Lurgi) Circulating Fluid Bed (CFB) calciner. Both are proven at about 3,000-4,500 t/d per unit with similar fuel use (about 2.8-3.1 GJ/t). GSC was chosen for three reasons. (a) Its stages suit the training curriculum: venturi flash dryer, 2 preheater cyclone stages, stationary furnace, holding vessel, 4 cooling-cyclone stages, fluid bed cooler and ESP. (b) The whole gas path runs under suction from one ID fan, so there are no high-pressure primary-air blowers and dust cannot leak outward. (c) It holds little material, so it starts and stops quickly. CFB differences are noted under 'alternatives'.
STEP 0 - Hydrate buffer (15-TK-001/002): Normally, product hydrate slurry from the A13 product classification goes straight to the A14 product filters. When one calciner is down (refractory relines take about 2-3 weeks per unit per year, plus trips), the shortfall is about 3,500 t/d of dry hydrate. That slurry (about 40-50 wt% solids in spent liquor) is diverted to two agitated storage tanks, which hold about 4-5 days of the shortfall. Afterwards it is pumped back to the product filters at a controlled rate while both calciners run at up to about 110-121 % of average demand. Outages longer than the buffer need a planned cut in refinery rate.
STEP 1 - Feed: Washed hydrate filter cake from the A14 product hydrate filters falls by chute or short belt into each train's calciner feed bin. The cake is at 6-10 % free moisture and 50-80 degC, with about 0.20-0.30 % Na2O on a dry hydrate basis and d50 about 80-100 um. Twin variable-speed screw feeders meter it into the venturi flash dryer.
STEP 2 - Drying (stage A01/P01): Gas leaving preheater cyclone P02 at about 350-420 degC enters through a venturi throat at the bottom of the dryer riser. It lifts the hydrate and the free moisture flashes off in about 1-2 s. Two dryer cyclones (P01) separate the dried hydrate at about 140-170 degC. The gas (about 140-170 degC, about 45-55 vol% H2O) goes to the ESP, then the ID fan, then the stack.
STEP 3 - Preheating and partial dehydration (P02): P01 solids are injected into the riser duct that carries furnace gas (about 950-1050 degC) from the P04 cyclones. In about a second they reach about 320-400 degC and start to dehydrate: 2 Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3 H2O(g). The reaction absorbs about +205 kJ/mol, or about 2.0 GJ/t Al2O3 including vaporising the water (thermochemical calculation from standard heats of formation). The heat in the furnace gas limits how far it goes in P02. A heat balance gives roughly 35-60 % of the bound water released here, with solids LOI falling from 34.6 % to roughly 15-25 % (engineering estimate). Furnace and HV complete the rest. Fine particles heated fast go gibbsite -> chi-alumina, while coarse particles in humid gas partly go to boehmite (AlOOH) first.
STEP 4 - Calcination (P04 furnace): The partly dehydrated solids enter the lower cone of the refractory-lined stationary furnace. Combustion air from cooling cyclone C01 arrives at about 650-800 degC. Natural gas is injected through a ring of burners in the cone and burns with the solids in suspension. Gas and solids leave the top at about 950-1050 degC, a set point that controls LOI and BET, with 2-4 % excess O2. Gas residence time in the furnace is only about 1-3 s. The furnace separation cyclones (P04) split the solids from the gas, which goes on to P02 (step 3).
STEP 5 - Holding vessel (HV): Solids from P04 drop into an air-fluidised, refractory-lined holding vessel. They stay about 10-30 min (engineering estimate) at about 920-1000 degC, which finishes the last hydroxyl removal. With the HV the furnace can run about 50-100 degC cooler than a GSC without one for the same LOI (vendor claim). That gives higher BET, lower alpha-alumina and lower fuel use. HV off-air returns to the furnace.
STEP 6 - Suspension cooling (C01-C04): Hot alumina passes counter-current through 4 cooling-cyclone stages. The ID fan draws ambient air, plus the FBC exhaust air, in at the C04 riser. The air takes up heat stage by stage and becomes the furnace combustion air. Alumina cools from about 950-1000 degC to about 180-280 degC, and the air heats from about 30-60 degC to about 650-800 degC. In this service the air carries about 15-20 % more heat per degree than the alumina (about 125,000-145,000 Nm3/h of air vs 146 t/h of alumina per train). An ideal 4-stage balance therefore gives at most about 730 degC air and about 160 degC alumina, and real stages fall a little short of that (engineering estimate).
STEP 7 - Fluid bed cooler (FBC): Alumina from C04 enters a multi-compartment air-fluidised bed. Water-cooled tube bundles immersed in the bed bring it to about 70-90 degC (duty about 5-8 MW per train). The heat goes through plate heat exchangers to make hot wash water for the hydrate filters, with a cooling tower as trim. Warm FBC exhaust air goes into the C04 air inlet so its heat is recovered.
STEP 8 - Product: The FBC overflows into airslides feeding the dense-phase conveyors to the product silos (A16). An auto-sampler takes samples for LOI, MOI, BET, alpha, PSD, Na2O and impurities and makes hourly composites.
PHASE CHEMISTRY: Gibbsite goes to chi or boehmite, then gamma, delta and theta (the transition aluminas, BET 60-80 m2/g in SGA), and finally alpha (corundum). Alpha forms significantly only above about 1100-1200 degC and is held below about 10 % in SGA, because it dissolves slowly in cryolite and lowers HF scrubbing capacity at the smelter. Raising calcination temperature lowers LOI and BET and raises alpha. Holding solids longer at moderate temperature (the HV) lowers LOI and keeps BET high.
HIGH-TEMPERATURE (BOEHMITIC) PLANTS: they use the same calciner technology. The differences are upstream: digestion at 240-270 degC with flash/heat-recovery trains. Hydrate quality depends on precipitation practice, not on the digestion route.
GAS SIDE: the whole GSC gas path is under negative pressure, from about -0.5 kPa at the C04 air inlet to about -9 to -13 kPa at the ID fan inlet (engineering estimate). That covers 7 cyclone stages in series plus the venturi, furnace, ESP and ducts. The ESP outlet dust limit is 30-50 mg/Nm3 (typical licence, set by jurisdiction). The off-gas is very humid (dew point about 78-85 degC), so all ducts, the ESP and the stack must run well above about 120 degC.

areas.name: Product Storage & Conveying
areas.purpose: Move hot SGA gently from the calciner fluid bed coolers to the refinery product silos and store ~7 days of production. Keep off-spec material separate, including returns from the port. Reclaim product to the covered overland conveyor to the port, with an optional road-tanker loadout. Main design constraints: low particle attrition (to protect the -45 um specification), no moisture pick-up or contamination (Fe, Si, organics), and enclosed, dust-free handling.
areas.process_description: 1) Each FBC discharges into an enclosed airslide feeding a twin-vessel dense-phase pneumatic conveying system, one line per calciner. 2) Dense-phase conveying moves alumina at low velocity (~3-10 m/s, engineering estimate) with high solids loading, which limits particle breakage. Lean-phase airlifts are avoided where possible because they make fines. 3) The pipelines discharge at the silo roofs into 2 x 20,000 t concrete product silos (40,000 t, ~7 days). A diverter can send start-up or off-spec alumina (e.g., high LOI after a trip) to a 3,000-5,000 t off-spec silo. That silo also takes rejects trucked back from the port, and its contents are reprocessed in controlled amounts through the calciner (P02 return) or into digestion. 4) Silo vent air (conveying air) passes through pulse-jet bag filters, and the dust returns to the silo. 5) Silo bottoms have aerated sectors (sequential aeration) with flow-control gates discharging into airslides and onto an enclosed 1,200 mm reclaim belt conveyor. The conveyor carries a belt scale, a self-cleaning magnet (protects the Fe spec) and a sampler. 6) The reclaim conveyor feeds the covered 1,200 mm overland conveyor to the port (A17), ~8 km (coastal-refinery basis, as at Alunorte-Vila do Conde, Gove and QAL). It is designed for ~800 t/h and runs ~8-10 h/d. 7) An optional road tanker loadout serves domestic smelters. SGA properties that matter: loose bulk density ~0.95-1.05 t/m3, angle of repose ~30-35 deg, low surcharge angle on belts (~5-10 deg), very abrasive, fluidisable (Geldart A/B) and hygroscopic (MOI rises in humid air). All handling is therefore enclosed. Belts are sized for ~55-65 % of the CEMA/ISO 5048 cross-section at a 10 deg surcharge.

areas.purpose: Receive SGA by overland conveyor, store ~100,000 t at the port, and load bulk carriers (Handysize to Panamax) at ~2,000 t/h with enclosed, dust-controlled handling and trade-certified weighing and sampling. Receive bulk liquid caustic soda (50 % NaOH) and fuel oil/diesel from tankers at a common-user liquid berth, and quicklime by ship at a multipurpose berth (or by road), for transfer to the refinery and mine. areas.process_description: EXPORT: 1) The overland conveyor discharges at the port receiving tower onto a 1,200 mm silo-top conveyor with plough/diverter gates into 4 x 25,000 t concrete silos (100,000 t, ~18 days, ~1.5-2 cargoes). A reject diverter in the receiving tower can send wet or contaminated alumina to a reject bin. 2) For ship loading, two silos are reclaimed together through aerated bottoms and flow-control gates onto a 1,600 mm reclaim conveyor. It feeds a ~300-500 t aerated surge bin in transfer tower TT-002, whose flow-control gate sets a steady rate onto the jetty conveyor. The jetty conveyor runs in an enclosed gallery with a closed floor and spill trays on a trestle. It feeds the wharf conveyor, whose tripper feeds the travelling shiploader. 3) A trade-certified belt weigher (OIML R50) and a primary cross-stream sampler (ISO 2927 principles) on the jetty conveyor give the shipping weight and the quality-certificate sample, and draft surveys confirm the weight. 4) The rail-mounted, luffing and telescopic (shuttle) shiploader moves between hatches. Its telescopic cascade chute with dust extraction places the alumina low in the hold to reduce dust and aeration. Holds must be clean and dry. Alumina (IMSBC Code group C) flows freely when aerated and must be trimmed. No water sprays are used on the product (moisture spec): dust control is by enclosure and bag filters. 5) Typical vessels are Handysize/Supramax of 25,000-60,000 DWT (cargo ~30,000-55,000 t), with Panamax of 65,000-80,000 DWT as the design vessel (laden draft up to ~14.5 m); ~40-60 shipments/yr. areas.name: Evaporation
areas.full_name: A18 Evaporation (spent liquor concentration: multiple-effect falling-film evaporators with feed flash, product flash and liquor inventory storage)
areas.purpose: Remove the water that enters the liquor circuit so the circuit stays in water balance. Sources are bauxite moisture, residue and hydrate wash water, lime slurry water, direct-steam condensate and gland/flush water. Part of the spent liquor is concentrated from ~245 to ~300-320 g/L caustic (as Na2CO3) and blended back to make digestion liquor at C ~270-290 g/L. Clean steam condensate is recovered for boiler feed and hot process condensate for washing. A caustic liquor inventory is held so that an evaporator-train descale or a digestion outage does not force a refinery rate cut. Design duty: ~420 t/h water evaporated (~1.75 t per t Al2O3) in 2 parallel trains of ~210 t/h. CHANGED from the draft: LP steam is ~112 t/h (range 100-125) instead of ~100 t/h, and steam economy is ~3.6-4.0 (including feed flash and product flash) instead of 4.0-4.5. The reason is a stage-by-stage heat balance of the backward-feed train (see process description item 3a).
areas.process_description:
1) Spent-liquor routing (A11/A18 interface decision). All spent liquor from precipitation/classification (A12/A13, ~3,050 m3/h at ~56-62 degC) first passes the A11 pregnant-liquor/spent-liquor heat interchangers. These add ~95-110 MW and the liquor leaves at ~80-88 degC. It then collects in two evaporator feed tanks (18-TK-001/002). About 55% (~1,700 m3/h) goes to evaporation. The other ~1,350 m3/h bypasses evaporation and goes to the digestion liquor blend tanks (18-TK-021/022). The A19 oxalate-depleted liquor (~300-400 m3/h, 45-50 degC) also returns to the feed tanks. Fine hydrate in spent liquor seeds gibbsite scale, so the feed is drawn from well-clarified overflow and the tanks are only gently agitated.

2) Backward feed with feed flash. Each train's feed pump (18-PP-001..004) delivers ~850 m3/h to the separator of effect 6, the coldest effect (~0.17-0.22 bar(a), liquor ~60-65 degC). The feed enters through a tangential flash inlet and flashes ~20 K, releasing ~30 t/h of vapour per train to the surface condenser. A bleed from each effect's recirculation-pump discharge, under level control, moves the liquor forward to the next hotter effect (6->5->4->3->2->1).

3) Each effect is a vertical falling-film calandria (18-EV-1x1..1x6). The recirculation pump lifts liquor to the distributor on the top tube sheet. The liquor runs down the inside of 10-12 m tubes as a thin film, heated by vapour condensing on the shell side. The water vapour released travels down the tube with the film and separates in the effect's vapour separator (18-VS). It then passes a chevron/mesh demister and heats the shell of the next colder effect. Effect 1 is heated by LP steam at 4-5 barg, desuperheated to ~5-10 K superheat. Typical temperature cascade: steam ~152-158 degC; liquor in effect 1 ~135-140 degC; ~10-12 K effective driving force per effect; boiling-point rise of Bayer liquor ~5-10 K per effect; last-effect vapour ~50-55 degC.

3a) Heat-balance note (why economy is ~3.6-4.0 and not ~5). The liquor-to-evaporation mass ratio is ~5:1 (~1,100 t/h liquor per ~210 t/h water per train). In backward feed every effect must also heat the incoming liquor by ~12-15 K. That sensible heat takes ~15-20 t/h of vapour equivalent per effect. The product flash and feed flash recover only part of it. Higher economy would need a 7th effect, product flash extended to ~80 degC, or mechanical vapour recompression (MVR) on the cold effects, all to be confirmed with the vendor.

4) Product liquor leaves effect 1 at ~135-140 degC and C ~300-320 g/L. It flashes through 4 product flash tanks (18-FT, ~10-11 K per stage) down to ~95-100 degC. Each tank's flash vapour joins the shell side of the matching effect (effects 2-5).

5) The strong liquor goes to the blend tanks (18-TK-021/022). There it is mixed with bypass spent liquor, 50% caustic make-up (A19) and the A19 causticised/purified returns to give digestion liquor (C ~270-290 g/L, A/C 0.36-0.38). The blend is pumped to the A06 digestion liquor tank and the A04 mill liquor tank. Two large liquor inventory tanks (18-TK-051/052) hold strong liquor and absorb dilute spent liquor during a train descale (~24-48 h) or a digestion outage, so the caustic concentration to digestion can be held.

6) Last-effect vapour and feed-flash vapour condense in a shell-and-tube surface condenser (18-CD-101/201) cooled by cooling-tower water. Liquid-ring vacuum pumps (18-VP) remove non-condensables (air, CO2, light organics/VOCs).

7) Condensates. Effect-1 steam condensate is clean. Conductivity and sodium analysers check it before it returns to the power house (A20), and it dumps automatically to process condensate if contaminated. Vapour condensates from effects 2-6, the flash tanks and the condenser carry trace caustic (pH ~9-11) and volatile organics. They are flashed through a cascade of condensate pots and collected in 18-TK-012. This is the single plant process-condensate (hot wash-water) tank, and it also receives the A07 flash-heater condensate (~230 t/h). areas.name: Liquor Purification
areas.full_name: A19 Liquor purification (causticisation, oxalate removal, organics removal by liquor burning, caustic make-up)
areas.purpose: Hold liquor impurities at steady, acceptable levels and maintain the caustic inventory. (1) Causticisation: convert sodium carbonate back to caustic with slaked lime, holding C/S ~0.86-0.90. The carbonate comes from bauxite carbonates, CO2 uptake and organic degradation. (2) Oxalate removal: crystallise and remove sodium oxalate before it co-precipitates with gibbsite, which causes fines, poor hydrate quality and high soda in the product. (3) Organics (TOC) removal: destroy humic and other organics that raise viscosity, cut precipitation yield, discolour hydrate and stabilise oxalate. This uses a side-stream liquor burning facility (LBF), which also destroys the oxalate cake. (4) Caustic make-up: receive (by pipeline from the port), store and dose 50% NaOH to replace soda losses (~75 kg NaOH/t Al2O3). CHANGED from the draft: causticisation duty is ~25 kg Na2CO3/t (was 35) on a ~600 m3/h side-stream (was 500), because the carbonate in dilute washer liquor was overstated.
areas.process_description:
1) Causticisation (side-stream on dilute liquor, improved two-stage scheme).
A side-stream (~600 m3/h, range 450-750) of residue washer 1 overflow (C ~110-130 g/L as Na2CO3) goes to the causticisation feed tank at ~85-95 degC. It may be blended with washer 2 overflow, giving C 90-130 g/L. Washing dilutes the liquor but does not change C/S (~0.86-0.88), so the carbonate is only ~14-20 g/L as Na2CO3. Dilute liquor is used because the carbonate-hydroxide equilibrium favours conversion at low caustic concentration.
Reactor 1 (19-TK-111) receives slaked lime slurry from the A20 ring main and runs close to the feed temperature (~75-90 degC, short residence ~15-30 min). There the lime reacts with aluminate and carbonate to form hydrocalumite: 4 Ca(OH)2 + 2 NaAl(OH)4 + Na2CO3 -> Ca4Al2(OH)12.CO3.xH2O + 4 NaOH.
The slurry is then heated by direct steam injection (19-SI-101, ~8-15 t/h LP steam) to ~100-103 degC in Reactors 2-3 (19-TK-112/113, ~1.5-2 h). There the hydrocalumite reacts with more carbonate to give calcium carbonate and release aluminate: Ca4Al2(OH)12.CO3 + 3 Na2CO3 -> 4 CaCO3 + 2 NaAl(OH)4 + 4 NaOH. The net reaction is Ca(OH)2 + Na2CO3 -> CaCO3 + 2 NaOH.
The competing reaction to avoid is 3 Ca(OH)2 + 2 NaAl(OH)4 -> Ca3Al2(OH)12 (tricalcium aluminate, TCA) + 2 NaOH. It wastes lime and alumina, and it forms if hydrocalumite is held too long or too hot in high-aluminate liquor.
Carbonate falls by ~9-12 g/L (product C/S ~0.93-0.95). Carbonate removed is ~6 t/h Na2CO3 (~25 kg/t Al2O3; range 15-40). Lime efficiency is ~50-65% for conventional single-stage causticisation and ~80-90% for the improved scheme (licensor data, verify). Design uses ~75%, giving ~4.2 t/h CaO.
The causticised slurry (~6.5-7.5 t/h solids, mostly CaCO3) returns to the residue washer train (A08, washer 3 feed). The CaCO3 leaves with the residue, and the regenerated caustic is recovered up the washer train.

2) Oxalate removal. Sodium oxalate forms when humic organics degrade (in the bauxite and in digestion). It builds up to its critical stability limit (~3-5 g/L in spent liquor, depending on C, temperature and organics), above which it co-precipitates on the hydrate as fine needles. At this plant:
(a) Controlled co-precipitation onto the fine/tertiary seed is washed off with hot condensate in A13 seed washing, giving an oxalate-rich seed-wash liquor (~150 m3/h, Na2C2O4 ~5-10 g/L).
(b) This liquor is mixed with a side-stream of strong evaporated liquor (~150-250 m3/h). The high caustic lowers oxalate solubility (salting-out). The mix (~300-400 m3/h, C ~190-220 g/L, ~85-95 degC) is cooled to ~45-50 degC in wide-gap plate coolers (~15-20 MW) and crystallised in seeded, agitated crystallisers (19-CR-201/202, ~4-8 h, oxalate seed ~20-50 g/L). The mix A/C is kept at or below ~0.40 to limit gibbsite co-precipitation.
(c) A thickener separates the crystals. Most of the underflow is recycled as seed, and a bleed is filtered on a horizontal vacuum belt filter. The overflow (Na2C2O4 lowered by ~1.5-2.5 g/L) returns to the evaporator feed.
(d) The oxalate cake (~0.6 t/h Na2C2O4, equal to the net oxalate generation, plus adhering liquor) goes to the liquor burner, where 2 Na2C2O4 + O2 -> 2 Na2CO3 + 2 CO2. Sodium oxalate also decomposes above ~290 degC to Na2CO3 + CO.
Alternatives used in industry: lime destruction (Na2C2O4 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaC2O4 + 2 NaOH, with calcium oxalate disposed with residue) and biological oxalate destruction (reported at Worsley, WA - verify).

3) Organics removal: liquor burning facility (LBF). A strong-liquor side-stream (~15-25 m3/h, TOC ~20-30 g/L C) is concentrated in a forced-circulation evaporator (19-EV-301) to ~50-60% total solids. A pug mill mixes it with recycled burnt product and the oxalate cake into agglomerates, which are burned in a rotary kiln (19-KL-301) at ~900-1,050 degC (engineering estimate). The sodium organic salts oxidise (R-COONa + O2 -> Na2CO3 + CO2 + H2O). In the hot zone, sodium carbonate reacts with alumina from the dehydrated aluminate: Na2CO3 + Al2O3 -> 2 NaAlO2 + CO2. Carbonate soda is therefore returned as caustic-equivalent aluminate.
The burnt product is cooled, dissolved in lean liquor (19-TK-311) and returned to the circuit. Kiln off-gas passes dust collection (ESP or baghouse), then a regenerative thermal oxidiser (RTO) to destroy VOCs and odour (cf. the RTO at the Alcoa Wagerup liquor burning facility - verify), then the stack.
Alternatives: fluidised-bed liquor burners (cf. Alcoa Kwinana - verify) and wet oxidation (~250-280 degC, ~80-110 bar, O2), which is not selected because of high pressure, corrosion and cost. East Coast India bauxite is low in organics, so the LBF can be smaller or deferred. Darling Range bauxite is organic-rich, which makes the LBF essential.

4) Caustic make-up. 50% NaOH is imported through the port (A17, bulk storage at the port) and pumped through an ~8 km pipeline to the refinery storage tanks 19-TK-401/402. A road-tanker unloading bay is the back-up. Caustic is dosed on ratio control to the strong liquor blend tanks (A18). Design rate is ~18 t/h NaOH (100% basis) = ~36 t/h of 50% solution (~24 m3/h); range 55-110 kg NaOH/t Al2O3 depending on reactive silica. Soda losses are: DSP (~0.69 t Na2O per t reactive SiO2), soluble soda in residue, soda in product (~0.3-0.4% Na2O), and oxalate/LBF/spills.

Note for high-temperature plants: boehmitic plants run lower caustic and higher temperature and add lime in digestion (forming cancrinite/hydrogarnet, which lowers soda loss and improves boehmite extraction). Their lime use is often higher and their causticisation arrangement differs.

areas.purpose:
Supply the refinery's utilities:
- Steam: ~450 t/h normal, 470 t/h design (~1.9-1.95 t/t), at MP 10-12 barg and LP 4-5 barg.
- Electricity: ~57-62 MW for the refinery plus ~6-10 MW for mine, overland conveyor and port.
- Raw water (~650 m3/h) and demineralised water.
- Cooling water: ~16,000 m3/h circulating (design).
- Compressed and instrument air: ~10,000-12,000 Nm3/h.
- Slaked lime: ~32 kg CaO/t Al2O3.
- Natural gas: ~2,400-2,600 GJ/h.
CHANGED from the draft:
- Steam demand raised from 410 to 450-470 t/h (gibbsite dissolution endotherm in digestion; evaporator steam 112 t/h).
- HRSGs re-rated to ~95-100 t/h each and a third auxiliary boiler added, so steam capacity with the largest unit out (N-1) is ~500 t/h.
- Cooling water raised from 10,000 to ~16,000 m3/h (7-cell tower).
- Lime lowered from 40 to ~32 kg CaO/t.
The utilities are designed N+1 so that agitation and steam continue when a unit is lost. Settling of solids in precipitators and thickeners after a total power loss is one of the most costly refinery upsets.
areas.process_description:
1) Steam and power (cogeneration).
Two gas-turbine generators (~25-35 MW ISO class, ~80-100 kg/s exhaust at ~480-550 degC) exhaust into two single-pressure heat-recovery steam generators (HRSG) with duct burners. Each HRSG raises ~35-45 t/h unfired and ~90-100 t/h fired (duct-burner outlet <=850-900 degC) at ~63-65 bar(a) / 470-480 degC.
Check: 90 kg/s x ~1.15 kJ/kgK x (850 - ~140) K = ~73 MW; divided by ~2,800 kJ/kg = ~94 t/h. Reaching 150 t/h would need a fully fired water-wall HRSG, which is not selected.
Three gas-fired D-type package water-tube boilers (~150 t/h each, same steam conditions) make up the balance. Normally two fire at ~65-90% load and the third is on hot standby. Installed HP capacity is 2 x 100 + 3 x 150 = ~650 t/h. With the largest unit (one 150 t/h boiler) out, ~500 t/h remains, which covers the ~450-470 t/h demand.
HP steam passes through a back-pressure/extraction steam turbine generator (~40-50 MW), with MP extraction at 10-12 barg (~190 t/h to the digestion live-steam heaters) and LP exhaust at 4-5 barg (~260-280 t/h to evaporators, pre-desilication, causticisation, LBF concentrator, deaerators and tank heating). Pressure-reducing and desuperheating stations (PRDS) back up each level when the turbine is off.
Total generation (~100-110 MW) exceeds site demand (~65-72 MW), so ~35-40 MW is exported to the grid (gas cogeneration supplying Western Australian refineries, e.g. the Alinta Pinjarra cogeneration plant - verify). The site can island on grid failure.
Alternative, common at Indian refineries (Lanjigarh, Utkal, Damanjodi): coal-fired CFBC boilers with back-pressure turbines (higher CO2, ~0.8-1.0 t CO2/t alumina; needs a coal yard, ash handling and ESPs).

2) Boiler feedwater and condensate.
Clean condensate returns from the digestion live-steam heaters (~180-200 t/h), evaporator effect 1 (~112 t/h) and the LBF concentrator (~8-12 t/h), ~290-310 t/h in total. It is checked by conductivity and sodium analysers with automatic dump, then filtered and polished into the condensate tanks. Together with demineralised make-up (~120-180 t/h; direct-injection steam to pre-desilication, causticisation and hydrate wash heating is not returned), it is deaerated at ~1.5 barg / ~127 degC. The deaerators take ~45-50 t/h of LP steam.
Chemical treatment: oxygen scavenger, amine or ammonia for pH, and phosphate or all-volatile treatment as the boiler supplier specifies. Caustic ingress from a heater tube leak is the main boiler-chemistry risk (caustic gouging and caustic embrittlement).

3) Raw water.
Water is pumped from a dam or river (~10-30 km pipeline) into a lined raw-water storage pond (~7 days) and distributed to: cooling-tower make-up (~280-310 m3/h), the water treatment plant (clarifier, multimedia filters, RO, mixed-bed polishers -> demin; ~190 m3/h raw), firewater, potable, dust suppression, gland/seal water and residue-washing top-up. Most process wash water comes from process condensate (A07/A18, ~650 t/h) and recycled residue-area (RSA) decant/stormwater. Cooling-tower blowdown and RO reject go to residue washing. Fresh water is ~2.7 m3/t.

4) Cooling water.
A 7-cell (6+1) induced-draft counterflow cooling tower (~16,000 m3/h design, ~14,000 normal, range ~10 K) rejects ~165-185 MW. Users:
- Evaporator surface condensers ~50-60 MW
- Precipitation interstage coolers ~45-70 MW (design 60)
- A11 trim coolers ~15 MW
- Oxalate coolers ~15-20 MW
- A15 product fluid-bed coolers ~10-12 MW, if on CW
- Compressor, turbine lube and generator coolers ~10 MW
The water is treated against scale, corrosion and biofouling, with pH and conductivity monitored to catch caustic ingress from process exchangers.

5) Compressed air.
Four oil-free centrifugal compressors (3 duty, 1 standby, ~4,000 Nm3/h each at 8 barg) supply plant air (filter cake blowing, air lances, tools, pneumatic-conveying top-ups) and, through desiccant dryers, instrument air at -40 degC pressure dew point (ISO 8573-1 class 2 for water). Instrument air has priority, through a receiver with a non-return valve.

6) Lime.
Quicklime (CaO ~88-92% available) arrives by road bulk tanker (from the port or a regional kiln) and is blown pneumatically into 2 silos (~1,500 t each, ~14 days at ~8.6 t/h). It is slaked in 2 x 100% detention slakers with hot process condensate: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2, about -1.14 MJ/kg CaO (exothermic), slurry ~75-85 degC. The water:lime ratio is controlled to hold that temperature. Grit is removed, and the 15-20% slurry is stored and circulated round a ring main to causticisation (A19), TCA/filter-aid preparation (A10), digestion/pre-desilication (A05/A06, optional) and residue neutralisation.

7) Fuel.
Natural gas arrives by pipeline at a receiving station for filtration, heating, metering and pressure reduction: ~25-30 barg for the gas turbines and ~4-8 barg for the calciners, boilers, duct burners and kiln. Diesel is stored for the emergency generators, diesel firewater pumps and the mobile fleet.

8) Electrical.
A 132 kV grid connection and main substation, with 11 kV generation and distribution, 6.6/3.3 kV for large motors (mills, compressors, CW pumps, BFW pumps) and 415 V MCCs. Two emergency diesel generators support essential loads (control systems, lube oil, thickener rakes, selected agitators, lighting).

Note for high-temperature (boehmitic) plants: digestion needs steam at ~30-60 bar or molten-salt/hot-oil heating, so the steam cycle has a high-pressure process header and less back-pressure power per tonne of steam.

areas.layout_notes: The power house is a block ~170 m x 110 m beside the steam load centre. It holds the GTs, HRSGs, 3 auxiliary boilers, the STG hall, the deaerator bay, BFW pumps and condensate polishing. It is ~150-300 m from digestion (A06) and evaporation (A18), so the large-bore MP/LP headers stay short on the main pipe rack. The HRSG and boiler stacks (~40-45 m) are on the downwind side of the block. The main 132 kV substation sits next to the power house on the side away from the cooling tower, at least 100-150 m from it to avoid drift and mist on insulators. The cooling tower (7 cells in a row, ~110 m x 18 m, plus the pump pit) lies between precipitation (A12) and evaporation (A18) to keep the CW headers short. Its long axis is perpendicular to the prevailing wind, and it is >=30-50 m from buildings and air intakes. The compressor house is near the power house or the centre of air demand (hydrate filtration A14, calcination/pneumatic conveying A15/A16). The lime area (silos ~30 m tall, slakers, slurry tank) is a ~50 m x 40 m compound beside the refinery access road, near causticisation (A19) and clarification (A08/A10), with a tanker turning circle. The raw water pond (~160 m x 130 m) and water treatment plant are at a site high point or edge, with the firewater tanks and fire pump house nearby. The gas receiving station is at the site boundary near the pipeline entry, >=50-100 m from ignition sources, with gas lines to the power house and calciners on the rack. Diesel storage is next to the EDGs and the mobile-equipment refuelling bay. A main E-W pipe rack spine (~1.2-1.5 km) with N-S branches (2-4 tiers, +6 to +15 m) carries steam, condensate, CW, air, lime and gas to all areas.
